disprove.verb type: action — dynamic verb of demonstration, comfortable in the progressive (*they're disproving it point by point*). No stative or linking use.
disprove.transitivity: **transitive** — the object is a claim, theory, rumor, or alibi, and it is obligatory: *disprove her central claim*; ✗ *the lab disproved* is incomplete.
disprove.passive: **yes** — *nobody has disproved her central claim yet*, *by 1960 the idea had been disproven several times over*.

engrave.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: cutting a surface, making a printing plate, and fixing something in the memory.
engrave.transitivity: **both** — normally transitive (*engraved our initials inside the ring*), but the object drops when the technique is the point: *he engraves by hand*.
engrave.passive: **yes**, and the memory sense is nearly always passive — *that afternoon is engraved on my memory*; also *US currency is still engraved rather than photographed onto the plate*.

gnaw.verb type: action — dynamic and iterative (repeated small bites); the figurative *gnaw at* is just as dynamic, not stative.
gnaw.transitivity: **both** — transitive when a hole results (*something gnawed a hole in the bag*), intransitive with *on* or *at* when none does (*puppies gnaw on anything*, *doubt gnawed at him*).
gnaw.passive: **restricted** — fine with a real direct object: *the insulation has been gnawed through again*. The *gnaw at* pattern resists it: ✗ *he was gnawed at by doubt*.

grave.verb type: action — dynamic verb of carving, but archaic; only the participle *graven* is still in circulation, and it works as an adjective (*a graven image*).
grave.transitivity: **transitive** — the object is the lettering or the surface worked: *the mason graved the family name across the lintel*.
grave.passive: **yes**, and the passive is where the verb survives: *the motto was graven over the doorway*, *those letters had been graved into the stone centuries earlier*.

hew.verb type: action — dynamic throughout, the literal chopping and the figurative *hew to* alike. *Rough-hewn* is a fixed adjective, not a verb form in use.
hew.transitivity: **both** — transitive in the cutting senses (*hewed the beam square*, *hewed a path through the brush*), intransitive with *to* in the commoner figurative sense (*the committee has hewed closely to the original plan*).
hew.passive: **restricted** — yes for the literal sense: *the cabin walls were hewn from a single stand of pine*, *crews have hewn a road out of solid rock*. No passive of *hew to*: ✗ *the plan has been hewed to*.

melt.verb type: action — dynamic and ergative: the same event stated intransitively (*the ice melted*) or transitively (*melt the butter*). Never stative, never linking; *molten* is an adjective only.
melt.transitivity: **both** — intransitive with the thing that changes as subject (*all the snow has melted off the north slope*), transitive with a causer (*melt the butter first*, *they melted down the old trophies*).
melt.passive: **restricted** — natural for the transitive senses: *the trophies were melted down for the silver*. The intransitive senses have no passive at all: ✗ *the snow was melted away*, ✗ *the crowd was melted into*.

mow.verb type: action — dynamic; no stative or linking use anywhere in the entry.
mow.transitivity: **both** — the object is usual but optional: *mow the yard*, *mow the back forty for hay*, yet *I mow every other Saturday* is complete on its own.
mow.passive: **yes** — *the crew has mowed the ball field twice this week* → *the ball field has been mowed twice this week*; *machine guns had mowed down the first two waves* → *the first two waves had been mowed down*.

prove.verb type: **action** in the demonstrating senses (*prove a theorem*, *prove his doubters wrong*), but **linking (copular)** in sense 2, *turn out to be*: *the drive proved longer than the map suggested*, *the drug had proved safe*.
prove.transitivity: **transitive** in the demonstrating senses, object obligatory (*the prosecution never proved he was in the building*), often with a following complement (*proved his doubters wrong*). The linking sense takes a subject complement and no object: *that shortcut always proves to be slower*.
prove.passive: **restricted** — yes in the demonstrating senses: *no one has proved the conjecture*, *the estate had been proved in probate court*. **No** passive of the linking sense: ✗ *it was proved longer*, ✗ *safe was proved by the drug*.

reprove.verb type: action — dynamic verb of speech, formal in register; the participial adjective *reproving* (*a reproving look*) belongs to it.
reprove.transitivity: **transitive** — the object is a person or a practice, and it is obligatory: *reproved both attorneys*, *reproved the practice in a letter*; ✗ *the judge reproved* alone is incomplete.
reprove.passive: **yes** — *he had been reproved in front of the whole department*. Use *reproved* in the passive, never ✗ *had been reproven*.

rive.verb type: action — dynamic verb of violent splitting. Archaic in the base and past; what survives is the participial adjective *riven*.
rive.transitivity: **transitive** — the object is the thing torn apart: *lightning rived the oak from crown to root*, *frost has riven the ledge into loose slabs*.
rive.passive: **yes**, and the passive is where the verb actually lives today: *the congregation had been riven by the vote*, *the party has been riven over the same question for a decade*.

rot.verb type: action — dynamic process verb, fine in the progressive (*the posts are rotting*); ergative like *melt*. *Rotten* is an adjective, not a working participle: ✗ *the boards have rotten*.
rot.transitivity: **both** — chiefly intransitive (*the apples rotted on the ground*, *he can rot in there*), transitive only with damp, water, or sugar as the causer: *water has rotted the sill under the window*.
rot.passive: **restricted** — the causative use passivizes weakly, and *was rotted* there reads half-adjectival: *the sill had been rotted by years of runoff*. The intransitive senses have no passive: ✗ *the apples were rotted on the ground*.

saw.verb type: action — dynamic. Note that the base is also the past of *see*, an unrelated verb: ✗ *I sawed a movie last night* wants *I saw a movie*.
saw.transitivity: **both** — transitive (*sawed the branch off flush with the trunk*, *the mill saws two hundred logs a day*), intransitive with *at* or *away* (*he sawed at the steak with a butter knife*, *the fiddler saws away for three hours*).
saw.passive: **restricted** — yes for the transitive senses: *someone had sawed off the padlock* → *the padlock had been sawed off overnight*. No passive of *saw at the steak* or of the slang *saw logs*: ✗ *logs were being sawed by Dad* is not the idiom.

sew.verb type: action — dynamic; no stative or linking use.
sew.transitivity: **both** — the object is usually present (*sew a straight seam*, *sew the button back on*, *sew up this tear*), but drops freely when the skill is the point: *she can sew*.
sew.passive: **yes** — *the costumes had been sewn by volunteers*, *the gash had been sewn shut*. The *settle, secure* idiom takes *sewed*: *by March they had the contract sewed up*, not ✗ *sewn up*.

shape.verb type: action — dynamic in both the physical sense (*shape the loaves*) and the influencing sense (*that summer shaped every decision*); *shape up* is dynamic too.
shape.transitivity: **transitive** in the main senses, object obligatory (*the wind shaped the dunes*; ✗ *bakers shape every morning* is incomplete). The phrasal *shape up* is intransitive: *he shaped up fast*, *this is shaping up to be the driest June on record*.
shape.passive: **yes**, and the influencing sense is frequently passive: *the policy had been shaped by a single lawsuit*. Never ✗ *has shapen* — the -n form survives only inside *misshapen*.

shave.verb type: action — dynamic; no stative or linking use. *Shaven* is an adjective (*clean-shaven*), not a working participle.
shave.transitivity: **both** — transitive (*shaved his beard off*, *shaved four dollars off the ticket price*, *the bus shaved the curb*), intransitive with no object at all: *I shave every other morning at most*.
shave.passive: **yes** — *the reed is shaved until it plays cleanly*, *points had been shaved in four games*. Use *shaved* in the perfect and passive: ✗ *he has shaven* sounds wrong to American ears.

shew.verb type: action — dynamic, exactly like *show*; this is an old spelling of that verb, not a separate one. Archaic register only.
shew.transitivity: **ditransitive**, as *show* is — *shew mercy to the people*, *shew someone the way* — and plain transitive elsewhere: *the old ledger shews every payment*.
shew.passive: **yes**, on the same terms as *show* — *editors have shewn it that way in every reprint*, *the manuscript had shewn the same reading*. In anything you write yourself, use *show*.

show.verb type: action — dynamic. Sense 6, *be visible*, is closer to a state but still takes the progressive (*she's starting to show*), so it is not a true stative.
show.transitivity: **ditransitive and more** — two objects (*show me the photo* / *show the photo to me*), plain transitive (*the audit showed no missing funds*), and intransitive in the *be visible* sense (*the stain doesn't show under the rug*).
show.passive: **yes**, and either object can become the subject: *both witnesses were shown the same lineup*, *her work has been shown in three cities*, *he hates being shown up in front of his kids*. No passive of the intransitive *the stain doesn't show*.

sow.verb type: action — dynamic in the farming sense and in the figurative *sow doubt* alike; no stative or linking use.
sow.transitivity: **transitive**, with either the seed or the ground as object: *sowed rye across the whole back field*, *sowed the north forty in clover*. The object drops when the method is the point: *she sows by hand*.
sow.passive: **yes**, and it is the usual shape of the figurative sense: *doubt had been sown long before the vote*; also *the terraces had been sown with barley for centuries*.

strew.verb type: action — dynamic verb of scattering. Unlike most of this group it keeps a live -n participle: *strewn*, not ✗ *strewed with paper*.
strew.transitivity: **transitive** — either the scattered things (*they strew sawdust on the floor*) or the covered surface (*every draft he strews with footnotes*) can be the object.
strew.passive: **yes**, and the passive is the commonest shape of the verb: *the shoulder of the road was strewn with glass*, *his career is strewn with abandoned projects*.

swell.verb type: action — dynamic process verb, fine in the progressive (*the crowd is swelling*). Not stative, despite the resultant adjective *swollen*.
swell.transitivity: **both** — overwhelmingly intransitive (*his ankle swelled within minutes*, *the chorus swelled until it filled the room*), transitive only with an external causer: *two good reviews have swelled his head*, *runoff swelled the channel*.
swell.passive: **restricted**, effectively no — the transitive use passivizes badly and *was swollen* reads as an adjective rather than an action: ✗ *his head was swelled by two good reviews*. The intransitive senses have no passive at all.

wax.verb type: **action** in the growing sense (*the moon waxed all week*) and in the polishing and depilation senses; **linking (copular)** in the fixed *wax poetic / lyrical / eloquent / nostalgic*, meaning *become* — and it will not extend past those collocations: ✗ *he waxed angry*.
wax.transitivity: **both** — intransitive in the moon and influence senses (*his influence has waxed and waned*) and in the linking use; transitive in the everyday senses: *I wax the car twice a year*, *she waxes her own eyebrows*.
wax.passive: **restricted** — yes for the *apply wax* and *remove hair* senses: *the floors were waxed before the open house*, *both her arms were waxed in twenty minutes*. **No** passive of the growing sense (it is intransitive) or of the linking one: ✗ *nostalgic was waxed by the critics*.

whipsaw.verb type: action — dynamic; the living American sense is figurative (hit from two directions at once), the literal woodworking one nearly obsolete.
whipsaw.transitivity: **transitive** — the object is the person, team, or market caught from both sides: *rising rates and falling rents whipsawed small landlords last year*.
whipsaw.passive: **yes**, and the passive is the normal form: *the team had been whipsawed by injuries on both lines*, *traders have been whipsawed by three straight reversals*. American English uses *whipsawed*, not ✗ *whipsawn*.

writhe.verb type: action — dynamic and strongly progressive-friendly: *he was writhing on the field for a full minute*. No stative or linking use.
writhe.transitivity: **intransitive** — it never takes an object; the cause follows a preposition: *writhe in pain*, *writhe with embarrassment*, *writhe through an interview*.
writhe.passive: **no** — an intransitive verb has nothing to promote to subject: ✗ *the field was writhed on*, ✗ *worse interviews have been writhed through*. The archaic *writhen* (*writhen roots*) is an adjective, not a passive participle.
